answer.rationale: The tempting move is the vendor switch: memory_c2 says exactly that worked, and the low-cost quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate. But c2 is the single memory carrying that recommendation, and what it actually attests to is cheap unit cost, fast onboarding, and clean invoicing — none of which is evidence about sustained delivery performance at committed volume. The line is at 94% with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days, so a switch would be a full-volume cutover with no fallback; c2's record was almost certainly written under slack conditions, which is why I want the archived source to see what utilization and volume it covered. I also verify c4 because it is the memory that carries my intended action, and I should not privilege the record that agrees with me: I need to know whether the recovered margin was a few points or something near 18%, since if it was small, negotiation alone cannot meet the mandate and the choice genuinely narrows. Negotiating is the one direction that pursues cost while keeping the incumbent's proven continuity (c1, c6) intact, and it is reversible — a failed negotiation still leaves the vendor switch and c3's second-source option live, whereas a failed cutover strands the line. Deferring (c5) does not apply: c5 concerned a non-critical service on month-to-month terms, while this contract does not auto-renew, so 'defer' here is really an unmanaged lapse. Standing uncertainty I am not resolving this cycle: whether the low-cost vendor can hold allocation at full committed volume, and whether the incumbent will move far enough on price to close the gap to 18%. I will carry the low-cost quote into the negotiation as documented leverage and record the residual gap so the next review can act on a second source rather than re-deriving this from scratch.
